sections.title: Executive summary

summary.text: Summarises global progress in National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) implementation across 206 countries, territories, and areas (including 98% of WHO Member States), estimating a global health and care workforce of 70.9 million in 2024 and highlighting workforce inequalities and ageing trends through 2030.

sections.extract: Over the last 20 years, there has been an increasing realization of the importance of having reliable and up-to-date data on the health and care workforce at the national level in order to understand the health labour market and to inform the development, implementation and review of health workforce (HWF) policies and plans. sections.title: Historical overview of health workforce data strengthening efforts

summary.text: Traces twenty years of global initiatives, World Health Assembly resolutions (including WHA63.16 and WHA69.19), and WHO guidelines from 2004 to 2023 that established and expanded the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) and human resources for health information systems.

sections.extract: 1.1 Historical overview of health workforce data strengthening efforts Since the onset of the 21st century, there has been an increasing impetus on the central role of health workers in developing and ensuring robust health systems and on the need for countries to mobilize resources to strengthen their health workforce (HWF), and in particular to generate robust HWF data and evidence (Fig. 1). sections.title: What is the NHWA?

summary.text: Defines the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) as a country-led system for progressively improving the availability, quality, and use of health workforce data across ten modules following the health labour market framework to support universal health coverage and the SDGs.

sections.extract: 1.2 What is the NHWA? The NHWA can be defined as a system by which countries progressively improve the availability, quality, and use of HWF data through monitoring of a set of indicators to support achievement of UHC, SDGs and other health objectives. Box 1 Core principles of the NHWA The core principles of the NHWA are as follows: • Multi-stakeholder and multi-sectoral governance mechanism of the national NHWA

sections.title: About this report

summary.text: Outlines the purpose and structure of this inaugural annual report on global and regional health workforce levels and trends, covering NHWA implementation progress, global and regional workforce estimates, demographic and workforce ageing analyses, and methodological annexes.

sections.extract: This report is the inaugural edition of an annual series on the levels and trends of the health and care workforce, based on the data shared by countries to WHO through the NHWA, and is intended to provide a snapshot of the current and past situation at the global and regional levels. sections.title: Status of health workforce data in 2025

summary.text: Analyses 2025 NHWA data availability, timeliness, periodicity, and disaggregation across indicators, occupations, and key health workforce topics, showing an nearly 20-fold increase in platform data volume from 12 587 data points in 2018 to 248 873 in 2025.

sections.title: Global and regional estimates

summary.text: Presents 2024 global, regional, and income-group stock and density estimates totaling 70.9 million health and care workers (15.1 million medical doctors, 31.0 million nursing personnel, 2.3 million midwifery personnel, 2.6 million dentists, 4.1 million pharmacists, and 15.7 million other occupations), highlighting stark regional and income-group disparities.

sections.title: Global and regional trends

summary.text: Examines global and regional trends in health workforce stock and density from 2006 to 2025, showing a 52% global increase in the combined density of SDG 3.c.1 occupations from 44.8 to 67.9 per 10 000 population alongside a projected global shortage of 11.1 million health workers by 2030.

sections.extract: The density of medical doctors, nursing and midwifery personnel, dentists and pharmacists has increased by 52% globally, from 44.8 per 10 000 population reported in 2006 to 67.9 reported in 2025, with the density of nursing and midwifery personnel increasing by nearly 60% (Table 4). sections.title: Global population demographic changes 2024–2030

summary.text: Illustrates 2024 global population age pyramids across World Bank income groups using UN World Population Prospects 2024 data, contrasting predominantly young populations in low-income countries with older populations in high-income countries.

sections.extract: 2024–2030 Fig. 16 illustrates the population age distribution of countries based on the World Population Prospects 2024 and highlights substantial differences by income group, with LICs characterized by predominantly younger populations and HICs by relatively older populations (46). sections.title: Health workforce ageing by occupation

summary.text: Compares the age profiles of medical doctors and nursing personnel across income groups, showing that high-income countries face higher proportions of health workers aged 55 years and older while low- and lower-middle-income countries have predominantly younger workforces under age 35.

sections.extract: The age distribution of health workers is linked to the age distribution of the total population, showing similarly younger health workers in LICs and older health workers in HICs. However, notable differences can be seen when comparing specific occupations, with medical doctors being older on average than nursing personnel (Fig. 17 (a) and (b)). sections.title: Health workforce gap due to population and health workforce ageing 2024–2030

summary.text: Projects the 2024–2030 health workforce gap arising from simultaneous population and workforce ageing, finding that 45 countries (including 17 in the WHO European Region) face declining workforce density by 2030 and estimating an additional need for 4.8 million health workers if age-specific utilization is accounted for.

sections.extract: health workforce ageing 2024–2030 The global HWF stock is projected to increase faster from 2024 to 2030 (16% increase) than the global population during the same period (5% increase). In the European Region and the Region of the Americas, where the combined HWF size is higher than other regions, the estimated increase of the HWF is smaller (6% in the Region of the Americas and 5% in the European Region). sections.title: Conclusion

summary.text: Synthesises the report’s findings on NHWA data improvements, persistent global workforce inequities, and demographic ageing pressures, calling for sustained investment in human resources for health information systems and strategic workforce planning.

sections.extract: Conclusion National health workforce accounts – health workforce levels and trends 2026 38 Over the last 20 years, data availability on various HWF characteristics have progressed substantially, in particular since the launch of the NHWA. sections.title: Annex 3: Methodology to estimate health workforce need

summary.text: Explains the double age-standardization methodology and country calculation example used to estimate 2030 health workforce requirements accounting for both population age structure shifts and age-specific health care utilization.

sections.extract: Methodology to estimate health workforce need Age-standardization of the health workforce need In the assessment of the impact of population ageing on the need, an age-standardization approach was used. The standardization was a double standardization on population age structure and on age-specific medical needs.
